raw_evidence.label: Catalog asymmetry: 391 vs 132
raw_evidence.content: The two artists are presented as peers but the data is structurally asymmetric. Beyoncé's lyric file contains 22,616 individual lines spread across 391 distinct song entries (including remixes, live cuts, medleys and a Lemonade film script). Taylor Swift's file contains 132 songs total, each as a single Lyrics blob, across 8 studio albums. After splitting Taylor's blobs into lines, Taylor totals 6,955 lyric lines — Beyoncé has 3.3 times as many lines on file. This is not because Beyoncé writes 3x as much per song; it is because her dataset includes every remix and live performance, while Taylor's is one canonical version per studio track.
raw_evidence.code:
charts = pd.read_csv(DATA / "charts.csv")

# strip column whitespace from Taylor's table
ts.columns = [c.strip() for c in ts.columns]
ts["Artist"] = ts["Artist"].str.strip()
ts["Album"] = ts["Album"].str.strip()
ts["Title"] = ts["Title"].str.strip()

# --- ana_01: Dataset shape summary ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
for name, df in [("beyonce_lyrics", bey), ("taylor_swift_lyrics", ts), ("sales", sales), ("charts", charts)]:
    print(f"{name}: rows={len(df)}, cols={len(df.columns)}, columns={list(df.columns)}")
print()
print(f"Beyonce unique songs: {bey['song_id'].nunique()}")
print(f"Beyonce avg lines per song: {bey.groupby('song_id').size().mean():.1f}")
print(f"Taylor songs: {len(ts)}")
print(f"Taylor unique albums: {ts['Album'].nunique()}")
print(f"Beyonce shows in beyonce_lyrics? {(bey['artist_name']=='Beyoncé').sum()} of {len(bey)} rows")

taylor_swift_lyrics: rows=132, cols=4
sales: rows=48, cols=8
charts: rows=140, cols=8
Beyonce unique songs: 391
Beyonce avg lines per song: 57.8
Taylor songs: 132
Taylor unique albums: 8

Contributors: Rosie Baillie and Dr. Sara Stoudt.
Includes beyonce_lyrics.csv, taylor_swift_lyrics.csv, sales.csv, charts.csv.
The readme directly invites users to replicate Rosie's tidytext analysis on Beyoncé.

sources.title: Rosie Baillie — Taylor Swift Lyric Analysis (RPubs)
facts: Rosie Baillie's original RPubs notebook is the seed analysis the dataset was built around.

raw_evidence.label: Why these two together
raw_evidence.content: Beyoncé and Taylor Swift were paired in the dataset because they are the two contemporary female solo artists most often invoked as the benchmark for cultural and commercial dominance in the 2010s — and because the 2009 VMAs incident (Kanye interrupting Taylor; Beyoncé later inviting her on stage) became one of the defining cultural beats that linked their careers in the public imagination. Both are also writers credited on most of their material, both have careers that span the rise of streaming, and both have been the subject of large amounts of fan-driven lyric annotation (which is why this Genius-derived dataset exists). The pairing isn't arbitrary; it's the comparison the culture has been making for a decade.

sources.title: E! News — The truth about the night Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift at the 2009 MTV VMAs
facts: Kanye West interrupted Taylor Swift's acceptance speech for Best Female Video at the 2009 MTV VMAs.
Kanye's protest was that Beyoncé's 'Single Ladies' video deserved the award.
Beyoncé later invited Taylor back on stage during her own win to give Taylor her moment.
The image of Beyoncé and Taylor Swift backstage at the 2009 VMAs is the cover image of the TidyTuesday readme.

raw_evidence.label: Catalog asymmetry: 391 vs 132
raw_evidence.content: The two artists are presented as peers but the data is structurally asymmetric. Beyoncé's lyric file contains 22,616 individual lines spread across 391 distinct song entries (including remixes, live cuts, medleys and a Lemonade film script). Taylor Swift's file contains 132 songs total, each as a single Lyrics blob, across 8 studio albums. After splitting Taylor's blobs into lines, Taylor totals 6,955 lyric lines — Beyoncé has 3.3 times as many lines on file. This is not because Beyoncé writes 3x as much per song; it is because her dataset includes every remix and live performance, while Taylor's is one canonical version per studio track.
raw_evidence.code:
charts = pd.read_csv(DATA / "charts.csv")

# strip column whitespace from Taylor's table
ts.columns = [c.strip() for c in ts.columns]
ts["Artist"] = ts["Artist"].str.strip()
ts["Album"] = ts["Album"].str.strip()
ts["Title"] = ts["Title"].str.strip()

# --- ana_01: Dataset shape summary ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
for name, df in [("beyonce_lyrics", bey), ("taylor_swift_lyrics", ts), ("sales", sales), ("charts", charts)]:
    print(f"{name}: rows={len(df)}, cols={len(df.columns)}, columns={list(df.columns)}")
print()
print(f"Beyonce unique songs: {bey['song_id'].nunique()}")
print(f"Beyonce avg lines per song: {bey.groupby('song_id').size().mean():.1f}")
print(f"Taylor songs: {len(ts)}")
print(f"Taylor unique albums: {ts['Album'].nunique()}")
print(f"Beyonce shows in beyonce_lyrics? {(bey['artist_name']=='Beyoncé').sum()} of {len(bey)} rows")

beyonce_lyrics: rows=22616, cols=6
taylor_swift_lyrics: rows=132, cols=4
sales: rows=48, cols=8
charts: rows=140, cols=8
Beyonce unique songs: 391
Beyonce avg lines per song: 57.8
Taylor songs: 132
Taylor unique albums: 8

Source: Genius API documentation (https://docs.genius.com/) Facts: Genius is the canonical source for crowd-sourced song lyrics with annotations.; Genius assigns numeric song_id and artist_id values, which match the columns in beyonce_lyrics.csv.

raw_evidence.label: Genius/lyric data origin
raw_evidence.content: The Beyoncé lyric file is one row per line of one song, identified by song_id and a song_line index — the format used by Genius's API and by the geniusr / genius R packages that wrap it. Taylor Swift's table is one row per song with the entire lyric blob in a Lyrics column, which is the format you get if you scrape lyric pages directly. This asymmetry matters for any analysis: Beyoncé's table is already pre-tokenized to lines (so 'how many lines does Halo have?' is a row count), while Swift's lyrics need to be split on newlines or tokenized before line-level questions are answerable. The scale gap is real — 22,616 Beyoncé lines vs Taylor's 132 songs — but it's an artifact of granularity and catalog scope, not a literal claim that Beyoncé wrote 22k more lines.

raw_evidence.label: Genius/lyric data origin
raw_evidence.content: The Beyoncé lyric file is one row per line of one song, identified by song_id and a song_line index — the format used by Genius's API and by the geniusr / genius R packages that wrap it. Taylor Swift's table is one row per song with the entire lyric blob in a Lyrics column, which is the format you get if you scrape lyric pages directly. This asymmetry matters for any analysis: Beyoncé's table is already pre-tokenized to lines (so 'how many lines does Halo have?' is a row count), while Swift's lyrics need to be split on newlines or tokenized before line-level questions are answerable. The scale gap is real — 22,616 Beyoncé lines vs Taylor's 132 songs — but it's an artifact of granularity and catalog scope, not a literal claim that Beyoncé wrote 22k more lines.

facts: Genius is the canonical source for crowd-sourced song lyrics with annotations.
Genius assigns numeric song_id and artist_id values, which match the columns in beyonce_lyrics.csv.

raw_evidence.label: Beyoncé's longest 'songs' are actually films and live shows
raw_evidence.content: Six of the ten longest entries in Beyoncé's lyric table are not pop songs at all — the longest is the 336-line script of the Lemonade film. Three entries are different live or remix versions of 'Get Me Bodied' (245, 195, and 195 lines), and the second-longest is a 253-line transcript of her 2014 VMAs medley. The first canonical solo studio track to appear in the top 10 by line count is 'That's How You Like It' (122 lines) with Jay-Z. This is a clue that Beyoncé's dataset has been padded out with performance and visual-album material that Taylor's, by construction, does not include.

raw_evidence.label: Signature hooks: 48 'how you like it's vs 12 'getaway car's
raw_evidence.content: When you ask each artist's lyric file 'what is the most-repeated single line within one song?', the answers describe two completely different songwriting modes. Beyoncé's top within-song repeat is 'That's how you like it, huh' — sung 48 times in a single track. Six of her top 15 most-repeated lines are 'If I let you go' (20 times each across multiple Ring The Alarm versions), and 'Who run the world? Girls!' takes the next three slots. Taylor's top within-song repeat is 12 — 'Look what you just made me do' (Look What You Made Me Do), 'Come back, be here', 'I'd never walk Cornelia Street again', 'Welcome to New York', 'In a getaway car', all tied. Beyoncé builds songs out of a single chant; Taylor caps her hooks at 12 because there is always another verse to come.
raw_evidence.code:
cnt = Counter(lines)
    for line, n in cnt.most_common(3):
        if n >= 4:
            ts_repeat_rows.append({"album": row["Album"], "title": row["Title"], "line": line, "repeats": n})
ts_repeat_df = pd.DataFrame(ts_repeat_rows).sort_values("repeats", ascending=False).head(15)
print()
print("Taylor — top 15 most-repeated lines within a single song:")
print(ts_repeat_df.to_string(index=False))

sentences.summary: det_05: tidytext as the canonical analysis style. Source: Text Mining with R — Sentiment analysis with tidy data (Silge & Robinson) (https://www.tidytextmining.com/sentiment.html) Facts: tidytext is built around the principle 'one token per row' (unnest_tokens).; AFINN, Bing, and NRC are the three lexicons most commonly demoed.

raw_evidence.label: tidytext as the canonical analysis style
raw_evidence.content: Rosie Baillie's RPubs notebook used the tidytext approach: lyrics → unnested into one-row-per-token, stop words filtered, then word frequencies, sentiment scores (with NRC, AFINN, or Bing lexicons), and tf-idf computed across albums. This is the analysis style the readme explicitly endorses and the audience expects. Two implications for downstream work: (1) word-frequency and sentiment-by-album are the well-trodden paths, so the most interesting findings will probably be the ones that contradict expectations (e.g. an album labelled 'breakup' that scores positive); (2) the AFINN/NRC sentiment lexicons systematically misread Black Vernacular English and slang ('bad' meaning 'good', 'killing it'), which is an important caveat when comparing Beyoncé's sentiment scores to Taylor Swift's.

raw_evidence.label: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with love-words
raw_evidence.content: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with classical 'love-words' (love, loved, loving, heart, baby, kiss) than Taylor Swift's. After removing stop-words and common filler, 2,925 of Beyoncé's 83,462 content tokens (3.50%) are love-words. Of Taylor's 23,596 content tokens, 556 (2.36%) are. Beyoncé's love-word rate is 1.5x Taylor's — the opposite of the popular framing of Taylor as the relationship songwriter. Taylor talks *about* love and breakups; Beyoncé writes inside the act, with a vocabulary saturated by physical presence ('baby' alone appears 1,024 times in her catalog).
raw_evidence.output:
Beyonce love-words: 2925/83462 = 3.50%
Taylor love-words: 556/23596 = 2.36%
Ratio Beyoncé/Taylor: 1.48x

raw_evidence.label: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with love-words
raw_evidence.content: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with classical 'love-words' (love, loved, loving, heart, baby, kiss) than Taylor Swift's. After removing stop-words and common filler, 2,925 of Beyoncé's 83,462 content tokens (3.50%) are love-words. Of Taylor's 23,596 content tokens, 556 (2.36%) are. Beyoncé's love-word rate is 1.5x Taylor's — the opposite of the popular framing of Taylor as the relationship songwriter. Taylor talks *about* love and breakups; Beyoncé writes inside the act, with a vocabulary saturated by physical presence ('baby' alone appears 1,024 times in her catalog).
raw_evidence.output:
Beyonce love-words: 2925/83462 = 3.50%
Taylor love-words: 556/23596 = 2.36%
Ratio Beyoncé/Taylor: 1.48x

raw_evidence.label: tidytext as the canonical analysis style
raw_evidence.content: Rosie Baillie's RPubs notebook used the tidytext approach: lyrics → unnested into one-row-per-token, stop words filtered, then word frequencies, sentiment scores (with NRC, AFINN, or Bing lexicons), and tf-idf computed across albums. This is the analysis style the readme explicitly endorses and the audience expects. Two implications for downstream work: (1) word-frequency and sentiment-by-album are the well-trodden paths, so the most interesting findings will probably be the ones that contradict expectations (e.g. an album labelled 'breakup' that scores positive); (2) the AFINN/NRC sentiment lexicons systematically misread Black Vernacular English and slang ('bad' meaning 'good', 'killing it'), which is an important caveat when comparing Beyoncé's sentiment scores to Taylor Swift's.

facts: tidytext is built around the principle 'one token per row' (unnest_tokens).
AFINN, Bing, and NRC are the three lexicons most commonly demoed.
Sentiment lexicons assign valence at the dictionary-word level and ignore context.

raw_evidence.label: Top non-stopword vocabulary
raw_evidence.content: Strip the function words and pronouns from each artist's catalog and a vocabulary footprint emerges. Beyoncé's top six content words are 'love' (1,362), 'baby' (1,024), 'see' (798), 'girl' (592), 'come' (566), 'want' (551). Taylor's top six are 'love' (248), 'never' (294), 'time' (225), 'back' (240), 'one' (178), 'say' (176). Both share 'love' and 'never' near the top — but Beyoncé's most distinctive frequent words ('baby', 'girl', 'boy', 'feel') run on body and presence, while Taylor's distinctive ones ('time', 'never', 'back', 'said') run on memory and reported speech. 'Halo' alone is sung 383 times across her dataset.

import math
def lr(b_count, t_count, b_tot, t_tot):

diff = []

    diff.append((w, bc, tc, lr(bc, tc, b_total, t_total)))

raw_evidence.label: Folklore is the only Taylor Swift album that goes net-negative
raw_evidence.content: Scoring each Taylor Swift album by (positive words − negative words) / total words × 100, every single album from 2006 through 2019 lands net-positive: the debut (+0.88), Fearless (+0.99), Speak Now (+1.02), Red (+0.92), 1989 (+0.77), reputation (+0.45), Lover (+0.41). Folklore, released in 2020 and written during lockdown, is the first and only Taylor Swift album to cross zero into net-negative sentiment: −0.21. The collapse is not noise — folklore has 140 positive words against 150 negative words, in 4,856 total words; every prior album has positive count exceeding negative. Speak Now (2010) is the most positive album she has made; folklore is the only sad one.

    pos, neg, total = 0, 0, 0

raw_evidence.label: Sales table provenance and limits
raw_evidence.content: The sales.csv table is derived from each artist's Wikipedia discography 'Sales' column, where studio albums report cumulative sales by country (US, UK, FRA, GER, etc.) plus a worldwide total ('WW'). These figures are not RIAA-audited point-of-sale numbers — they are the values Wikipedia editors aggregated from a mix of certifications, IFPI press releases, and earlier industry reports, which means they tend to be conservative for albums that kept selling after the table was last updated and inflated for albums where label PR seeded a high number that propagated. The implication: rank ordering across the artists' top albums is reliable; precise dollar values are not.

Source: Text Mining with R — Sentiment analysis with tidy data (Silge & Robinson) (https://www.tidytextmining.com/sentiment.html) Facts: tidytext is built around the principle 'one token per row' (unnest_tokens).; AFINN, Bing, and NRC are the three lexicons most commonly demoed. | det_08: Beyoncé palette — community signal that color matters here. Source: dill/beyonce — R package of Beyoncé color palettes (https://github.com/dill/beyonce) Facts: GitHub repository providing R color palettes derived from Beyoncé album visuals.; Linked directly from the TidyTuesday readme as a recommended companion package.

raw_evidence.label: tidytext as the canonical analysis style
raw_evidence.content: Rosie Baillie's RPubs notebook used the tidytext approach: lyrics → unnested into one-row-per-token, stop words filtered, then word frequencies, sentiment scores (with NRC, AFINN, or Bing lexicons), and tf-idf computed across albums. This is the analysis style the readme explicitly endorses and the audience expects. Two implications for downstream work: (1) word-frequency and sentiment-by-album are the well-trodden paths, so the most interesting findings will probably be the ones that contradict expectations (e.g. an album labelled 'breakup' that scores positive); (2) the AFINN/NRC sentiment lexicons systematically misread Black Vernacular English and slang ('bad' meaning 'good', 'killing it'), which is an important caveat when comparing Beyoncé's sentiment scores to Taylor Swift's.

facts: tidytext is built around the principle 'one token per row' (unnest_tokens).
AFINN, Bing, and NRC are the three lexicons most commonly demoed.
Sentiment lexicons assign valence at the dictionary-word level and ignore context.

raw_evidence.label: Beyoncé palette — community signal that color matters here
raw_evidence.content: There is an R package called `beyonce` whose entire purpose is to provide curated color palettes drawn from Beyoncé album covers and music videos. The TidyTuesday readme explicitly links to it. This is a small but telling signal: in the data-viz community, Beyoncé's catalog is recognised as a *visual* canon, not just a sonic one. Taylor Swift has parallel visual eras (the Eras Tour was built on it). For a designer, this is permission — and in fact, encouragement — to lean into album-cover-coded color palettes rather than defaulting to the Tableau-10 categorical scheme.
